title: Embedded frames need a title
summary: An iframe has no title, so screen reader users hear only "frame" and cannot tell what it holds. Add a short title that describes its purpose.
problem: An iframe shows another page inside yours, such as a map, a video or a booking form. Without a title attribute it has no accessible name, so assistive technology announces a generic frame with no hint of what is inside.
whoItAffects: People who use a screen reader often list the frames on a page and jump between them. With no titles they hear a row of identical unnamed frames and have to enter each one to find out what it is.
steps: Find the iframe named in the scan result. It is usually an embed code pasted in from a map, video or form provider.
Add a title attribute that says what the frame contains, such as title="Map showing our shop at 12 Mill Lane".
Keep the title short and specific. Words like iframe, embed or content tell the listener nothing.
If the page has several frames, give each its own title so they can be told apart.
after: <iframe src="https://www.google.com/maps/embed?pb=!1m18!1m12" width="600" height="400" title="Map showing Fernwood Garden Supply at 12 Mill Lane"></iframe>
whyItMatters: This is a WCAG 4.1.2 failure at Level A, Name, Role, Value. Embedded maps, videos and chat widgets are common places for it, because the embed code a provider gives you often has no title.
howToCheck: Inspect the iframe in your browser's developer tools and confirm it has a title that describes its content. The accessibility panel should show the same text as the frame's name.

platformNotes.note: If you paste an embed code into a Custom HTML block, add the title attribute to the iframe tag in that code, then update the page.
Embed codes usually live in a Custom Liquid section or a theme file. Add the title attribute to the iframe tag there.
